content: Acanthosis nigricans is characterized by areas of dark brown to black, poorly defined, and velvety hyperpigmentation of the skin. These changes are most commonly observed in the posterior and lateral folds of the neck, the axillae, the groin, the umbilical region, and other body folds. Involvement of mucous membranes is rare, but when present, it may indicate an associated malignant condition. Life-threatening causes of acanthosis nigricans include conditions that, if left untreated, could result in death or permanent disability within 24 hours. Common causes of acanthosis nigricans include diabetes mellitus, drug-induced cases, gastric cancer, idiopathic origins, insulin resistance, obesity, and polycystic ovary syndrome. Physicians can typically diagnose acanthosis nigricans through a visual examination of the skin. In atypical cases, a skin biopsy may be required. If the underlying cause is not immediately apparent, further diagnostic investigations may be necessary. These may include blood tests, endoscopy, or imaging studies such as X-rays to rule out diabetes or malignancy as potential causes. During a physical examination, the skin changes associated with acanthosis nigricans are noted. These findings are often documented with permission from dermatological resources, such as the Dermatology Atlas. Pseudocanthosis nigricans, a variant of the condition, is also documented in dermatological references, with similar visual characteristics but differing underlying causes. Treatment for acanthosis nigricans involves screening for diabetes and, in rare cases, cancer. Managing blood glucose levels through lifestyle modifications, including exercise and dietary changes, often leads to an improvement in symptoms. The prognosis for acanthosis nigricans is generally favorable. The condition often resolves or improves significantly if the underlying cause is identified and treated appropriately.
